text_nl:
Here is the conversion of each table row into exhaustive, searchable natural language:

The row describing "earnings of $5,500 from employment as a fisher" states that this rule applies only to those who have had minimal or no labour market attachment, meaning those who had less than $3,000 in earnings from employment as a fisher in the 52-week period prior to the qualifying period, where time on EI, workers’ compensation, disability benefits and sick leave counts as time worked, and the corresponding column value is empty.

The "Reduction in Maximum Insurable Earnings" indicates that the maximum insurable earnings (MIE) was reduced to $39,000 per year ($750 per week) in July 1996 and frozen at this level until 2006, which reduced the maximum weekly benefit to $413 (55% of $750), from $448 in 1995 and $465 for the first six months of 1996, because it adjusts the MIE to a level where Employment Insurance benefits would no longer be competitive with wages in some parts of the country and in some industries, and was based on a formula that took into account average wage increases over the eight years before the reduction, as the high inflation and wage increases of the 1980s continued to be considered in setting the MIE, it had escalated faster than wages.

The "Reduced Maximum Duration of Regular Benefits" specifies that effective July 1996, the maximum length of a claim was reduced from 50 to 45 weeks, reflecting the fact that most claimants find work within the first 40 weeks of receiving benefits.

The "Calculation of Weekly Benefit Rate" outlines that weekly benefits were calculated based on total earnings over the 26-week period preceding the establishment of the claim, divided by the number of weeks of work in this period or the minimum divisor of 14 to 22 (depending on the regional rate of unemployment), whichever is higher, with the result multiplied by 55% to determine the weekly benefit rate, which creates a strong incentive to work more than the minimum amount of time to qualify for benefits (at least two more weeks than the old entrance requirement) and provides an incentive to work in the “shoulder” season.

The "Family Supplement" states that claimants with children who receive the Canada child tax benefit and who have an annual family net income of up to $25,921 receive a top-up of their basic Employment Insurance benefits, and the Family Supplement increased the maximum benefit rate to 65% in 1997, to 70% in 1998, to 75% in 1999 and to 80% in 2000, which improves assistance to those most in need because the old 60% dependent rate under the Unemployment Insurance was very poorly targeted, with about 45% of low-income families not qualifying and about 30% of those who did receive the 60% rate having family incomes over $45,000.

The "Allowable Earnings While on Claim" indicates that effective January 1997, claimants can earn $50 or 25% of their weekly benefit rate, whichever is higher, without a reduction of their Employment Insurance benefits, whereas prior to 1997, the exemption was only 25% of the weekly benefit rate, which helps low-income claimants and encourages claimants to maintain work attachment and increase their earnings from work.

The "Benefit Repayment (Clawback)" specifies that benefits were repaid at the rate of $0.30 for every $1 of net income above the threshold, where for those who had collected 20 or fewer weeks of benefits in the last five years, the threshold was $48,750 of net income (the former level was $63,570) and the maximum repayment remained at 30% of benefits received, and for those with more than 20 weeks of benefits in the last five years, the threshold was $39,000 of net income and the maximum repayment varied from 50% to 100% of benefits received, depending on previous use, which makes benefits fairer and more accurately reflective of insurance principles, discourages repeated use of EI by those with high levels of annual income, and notes that the Benefit Repayment provision was revised in Bill C-2 (2001).

The "Intensity Rule" outlines that the intensity rule reduced the benefit rate by 1 percentage point for every 20 weeks of regular or fishing benefits collected in the past five years, with a maximum reduction of 5 percentage points, which introduces an element of experience rating to the program, since heavy users of the system bore more of the costs, discourages use of Employment Insurance as a regular income supplement rather than insurance for times of unpredictable job loss while not excessively penalizing those who make long or frequent claims, creates a better balance between contributions made and benefits received, and was repealed in Bill C-2 (2001).

text_nl:
The legislative change, effective January 1997, states that all earnings from the first dollar are insurable up to the maximum yearly insurable earnings, and there are no weekly minimums or maximums for determining earnings; this change creates a more equitable and balanced system where all earnings are insurable, decreases paper burden for employers, and helps guard against abusing the system to avoid paying premiums.
Regarding Premium Refunds, since 1997, workers earning $2,000 or less per year have had their premiums refunded; this helps workers who must pay premiums but do not have enough hours to qualify for benefits.
Regarding Increased Sanctions for Fraud, effective July 1996, penalties for fraud by employers and claimants were increased, and since January 1997, claimants who committed fraud after June 1996 have faced higher entrance requirements; this protects the integrity of the Employment Insurance program.
Regarding Part II of the Employment Insurance Act: Employment Benefits and the National Employment Service, Part II of the Employment Insurance Act provides authority for three types of arrangements for employment program implementation and delivery with support from EI funds; specifically, the Canada EI Commission is authorized to establish federal employment programs, coupled with a duty to work with provincial governments regarding their design, delivery and evaluation, to enter into agreements for the administration on its behalf of its employment benefits and support measures, and to enter into agreements with provinces, territories and other entities to contribute toward the costs of their similar benefits and measures programs (Labour Market Development Agreements/Indigenous Skills and Employment Training program agreements).
